The Mindanao treeshrew (Tupaia everetti) is a small-bodied scansorial mammal endemic to the montane forests of Mindanao Island in the Philippines. Field-based respirometry trials conducted on resting, post-absorptive individuals measured the species' basal metabolic rate at a maximum of 224.1 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 224.1 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when the ambient temperature was held at 35.7 °C [T = 35.7 °C], a value consistent with the moderate metabolic demands anticipated for an insectivorous mammal of this body size. Neonatal offspring emerge from the birth canal weighing approximately 20 grams [Wwb = approximately 20 grams], a mass that reflects the typical altricial condition of tupaiid newborns and which necessitates an extended period of maternal provisioning. The interval from conception to live birth, as documented in a captive breeding colony, spans 55 days [tg = 55 days] when females are maintained at a stable thermal environment of 35.7 °C [T = 35.7 °C], with individual records ranging narrowly between 54 and 56 days, suggesting a tightly canalized gestational program in this species.

Reproductive output in the Mindanao treeshrew is precisely timed under stable laboratory conditions. Under a consistent thermal environment of 35.7 °C [T = 35.7 °C], the maximum observed frequency of reproductive events is approximately two litters each year [F_R_i = approximately two litters each year], with each litter containing an average of 1 offspring [N_R_i = each litter containing an average of 1 offspring], yielding a conservative annual output consistent with the species' slow life-history strategy. The interbirth interval is correspondingly long, allowing females to invest considerable time and energy into gestation and subsequent lactation before initiating the next breeding cycle.

Puberty, marking the onset of gonadal maturation and the first capacity for gamete production, is attained at 90 days since birth [tp = 90 days since birth] in individuals housed under thermoneutral conditions at 35.7 °C [T = 35.7 °C]. This represents a relatively rapid developmental trajectory for a mammal of its ultimate body size, enabling young treeshrews to reach reproductive competence within their first three months of life. However, first successful copulation and subsequent pregnancy are often deferred beyond this initial physiological milestone, likely constrained by social dominance hierarchies and the need to establish a foraging territory within the dense understory of the montane forest. The comparatively early pubertal timing is hypothesized to facilitate rapid population turnover in a habitat where seasonal fluctuations in invertebrate prey abundance can strongly influence juvenile survival rates.

Developmental milestones during the early postnatal period have been precisely characterized in captive individuals. Under the same ambient temperature of 35.7 °C [T = 35.7 °C], weaning, defined as the cessation of lactation and the complete transition to solid food, occurs at 38 days since birth [tx = 38 days since birth], a duration that aligns with the extended period of maternal care observed in several other Tupaia species. The body mass of pups at this critical juncture, when they achieve nutritional independence, is approximately 104.5 grams [Wwx = approximately 104.5 grams], representing a substantial increase over the initial neonatal mass of 20 grams [Wwb = 20 grams]. This fivefold gain in body weight over a five-week period underscores the efficiency with which the mother's milk supports rapid somatic growth. Juvenile treeshrews then enter a sub-adult phase of independent foraging and continued skeletal development before reaching their full adult dimensions.

The ultimate wet weight, or asymptotic adult body mass, of the Mindanao treeshrew is recorded at approximately 355 grams [Wwi = approximately 355 grams], a moderate size for a member of the family Tupaiidae and one that places it within the typical range for diurnal, arboreally-foraging insectivores in Southeast Asian forests. Longevity records from both field and captive populations indicate that the maximum lifespan of this species is 11.5 years [am = 11.5 years] when animals are maintained at a controlled temperature of 35.7 °C [T = 35.7 °C], a notable duration for a mammal of this body mass and one that suggests a relatively slow pace of aging. Field studies on Tupaia everetti have further documented that home range size in males averages 2.3 hectares, overlapping with the smaller ranges of several females—a spatial arrangement consistent with dispersed-male polygyny, a common mating system among solitary forest insectivores.
